Design effect

Source: R/estimate.R
deff.Rd

How much precision the design costs against simple random sampling of the same size (Kish 1965). deff = 1 means the design is doing as well as a simple random sample from the rows it can reach; above 1 it is doing worse, which is the usual price of clustering; below 1 it is doing better, which is what stratification and probability-proportional-to-size buy you.

Usage

deff(object, ...)

Arguments

object

A result from ht_total(), ht_mean(), ht_ratio() or ht_quantile(), or an object from survey that holds a design effect.

...

Passed to survey::deff() for an object from survey, such as its quietly. Not used for an estimate made here.

Value

A single number, or NA when the design has no variance estimate, y is constant in the sample, or the estimate is a mean from ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE) with y missing in some sampled rows. For an object from survey, what survey::deff() returns.

Details

Read it as an exchange rate on sample size: at deff = 2, a sample of 400 carries about as much information as 200 drawn at random.

The simple random sample it is measured against is drawn from the rows the design gives a probability above 0, sum(inclusion_prob(design, frame) > 0) of them, because those are the rows a total or a Hajek mean estimates over. Rows past max_items, outside a region or time window, dropped by na_rm or in a stratum allocated no rows are left out. Counting them set an equal-probability sample of 20 from the first 100 rows of a 400-row frame at a design effect of 0.05 for a total, "better than simple random sampling", where the right figure is 1. survey measures against the sum of the weights, which is that count for an equal-probability design, and gives the same design effect there. A Horvitz-Thompson mean (estimator = "ht") divides the total by the frame's row count, so its design effect is the total's.

The design effect is NA when there is no variance, and when y takes one value in every sampled row, where there is no spread for a simple random sample to be measured by. It is NA too for a mean from ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE) with y missing in some sampled rows, since the rows with y are a domain of the sample, and a domain's design effect is not estimated.

A table of domain estimates from by, of several variables, of the levels of a factor or of quantiles carries no design effect, and deff() refuses it with a message saying so. A contrast's design effect is NA, and so is a quantile's from ht_quantile(). A ratio from ht_ratio(), and a total from the ratio estimator, are measured against the same estimator from a simple random sample, through the variance of its linearised residuals, as survey::svyratio(deff = TRUE) measures a ratio.

survey has a deff() of its own, and whichever of the two packages is attached last masks the other's. Either one answers for both. This deff() is a generic that passes an object it has no method for, such as survey::svymean(..., deff = TRUE), to survey::deff(), and survey's generic finds the methods for the estimates made here.

References

Kish, L. (1965). Survey Sampling. Wiley.

See also

ht_total(), ht_mean(), plan_size(), which takes a design effect as an input.

Examples

set.seed(1)
# Sites differ from each other, and rows within a cluster are alike --
# exactly the structure that makes stratifying pay and clustering cost.
pop <- data.frame(
  id = 1:400,
  site = rep(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), each = 100),
  cl = rep(paste0("c", 1:40), each = 10)
)
pop$y <- rep(c(20, 60, 120, 200), each = 100) + round(stats::rnorm(400, 0, 8))

# Stratifying on something that matters buys precision (deff below 1)
deff(ht_total(draw(pop, design_stratified("site", n = 40), seed = 1,
                   weights = TRUE), "y"))
#> [1] 0.01174153

# Clustering usually costs it (deff above 1)
deff(ht_total(draw(pop, design_cluster("cl", n_clusters = 4), seed = 1,
                   weights = TRUE), "y"))
#> [1] 12.91977
